Research questionHow did the 1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak, which started with children who were sick in Washington state, cause the government to change how ground beef is regulated, and what changed in how fast food is made and inspected after this incident?−

How did the 1993 Jack in the Box E. coli outbreak, which started with children who were sick in Washington state, cause the government to change how ground beef is regulated, and what changed in how fast food is made and inspected after this incident?

Chapter 03 · Evidence board

The evidence

Nineteen exhibits, each with a source and a limit. Follow the chain—but judge how much each link can carry.

E01—E19

Open the evidence files

Every file shows what the evidence says, why it matters, what it supports, and what it cannot prove.

19 exhibits
E01
1982–1983A rare E. coli strain is linked to fast-food hamburgersVERIFIED strong

Evidence
Two 1982 outbreaks of bloody diarrhea in Oregon and Michigan, affecting at least 47 people, were tied to restaurants of one fast-food chain. Investigators isolated E. coli O157:H7 from patients and from a beef patty.

What it tells us
O157:H7 was identified as a cause of foodborne illness, connected to hamburger patties, more than ten years before 1993.

Why it matters
The danger was known before the outbreak, so 1993 was not a total surprise to scientists.

Claim it supports
E. coli O157:H7 was recognized as a hamburger-associated threat by 1983.

Limitations
A medical study. It does not discuss regulation or how industry responded.

Full MLA source
Riley, Lee W., et al. “Hemorrhagic Colitis Associated with a Rare Escherichia coli Serotype.” New England Journal of Medicine, vol. 308, no. 12, 24 Mar. 1983, pp. 681–85. Source record ↗

Academic researchSciencescience timeline
E02
13 Jan. 1993A doctor reports sick children to the stateVERIFIED strong

Evidence
A physician reported a cluster of children with hemolytic uremic syndrome (HUS), a kidney complication, to the Washington State Department of Health.

What it tells us
The investigation began with a doctor noticing a pattern in sick children, not with meat inspection.

Why it matters
It shows how the outbreak was detected: through medicine and public health.

Claim it supports
The outbreak investigation started with a physician's report of children with HUS in Washington State.

Limitations
The CDC report does not name the physician, the hospital, or the counties involved.

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceOutbreakoutbreak map
E03
16–17 Jan. 1993Sick people had eaten at the same chainVERIFIED strong

Evidence
A case-control study implicated eating at “chain A” restaurants in the week before illness. 372 of 425 patients (88%) had eaten at chain A within 9 days of getting sick; 312 of 338 who remembered what they ate (92%) had a regular-sized hamburger patty.

What it tells us
Investigators connected the cases to one restaurant chain and one product within days.

Why it matters
This statistical link is what turned scattered illnesses into a single outbreak with a single source.

Claim it supports
Cases were linked to hamburgers from one restaurant chain.

Limitations
The CDC report calls the chain “chain A.” Naming it Jack in the Box relies on other sources, such as Bell et al. (1994) and Murano et al. (2018).

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceOutbreakoutbreak restaurants
E04
18 Jan. 1993The recall recovers about one in five pattiesVERIFIED strong

Evidence
A multistate recall began on 18 January. About 272,672 of the implicated patties, roughly 20%, were recovered.

What it tells us
Most of the contaminated meat had already been served or could not be found when the recall began.

Why it matters
It shows the limits of reacting after the fact, an argument later used for prevention-based rules.

Claim it supports
A recall began on 18 January 1993 and recovered about 20% of implicated patties.

Limitations
The report does not say who ordered the recall or how it was carried out.

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceOutbreakoutbreak government
E05
Jan.–Apr. 1993The meat came from many plants and farmsVERIFIED strong

Evidence
The outbreak strain was found in 11 lots of patties produced on 19 and 20 November 1992. Traceback pointed to five U.S. slaughter plants and one in Canada as likely sources, with animals from farms and auctions in six western states. No single plant or farm was identified.

What it tells us
One patty could contain meat from many animals and places, so a source was nearly impossible to pin down.

Why it matters
This is the industrial system that Juska et al. argue made outbreaks like this likely.

Claim it supports
Ground beef in the outbreak was traced to multiple slaughter plants and farms, not one source.

Limitations
It describes one product chain. It does not by itself prove the whole industry was riskier than before.

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceMeat industryindustry outbreak
E06
15 Nov. 1992 – 28 Feb. 1993Four states, four deathsVERIFIED strong

Evidence
Cases meeting the case definition: Washington 477, Nevada 58, California 34, and Idaho 14 culture-confirmed. Four people died: three in Washington and one in California.

What it tells us
The outbreak was centered on Washington but crossed into three more western states.

Why it matters
The scale and the deaths of children are why the outbreak drew national attention.

Claim it supports
The outbreak affected four western states and caused four deaths.

Limitations
Counts depend on the case definition. Other sources give different totals (see Sources Disagree).

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceOutbreakoutbreak map
E07
Apr. 1993Undercooking “likely played an important role”VERIFIED moderate

Evidence
The CDC wrote that undercooking of hamburger patties likely played an important role, and noted that the FDA had issued interim recommendations to raise the internal temperature of cooked hamburgers to 155°F.

What it tells us
Cooking temperature was identified as a key factor, and federal cooking guidance changed in 1993.

Why it matters
This is the direct answer to the hook: part of why your burger is cooked the way it is.

Claim it supports
Federal guidance raised the recommended cooking temperature for hamburgers to 155°F after the outbreak.

Limitations
“Likely” is the CDC's own hedge. The report does not give the chain's actual cooking temperatures.

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceRestaurantsrestaurants regulation
E08
Apr. 1993Officials were already working on “critical control points”VERIFIED moderate

Evidence
The CDC's editorial note stated that CDC was collaborating with USDA's Food Safety and Inspection Service to identify critical control points in processing, as part of a program to reduce pathogens such as O157:H7 entering the meat supply.

What it tells us
The prevention approach that became HACCP was already being discussed by federal agencies in 1993.

Why it matters
It complicates a simple story: the government was not starting from zero after the outbreak.

Claim it supports
Federal agencies were working on a critical-control-point approach in 1993.

Limitations
It does not say when this work began, or whether it started because of the outbreak.

Full MLA source
Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. “Update: Multistate Outbreak of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Infections from Hamburgers — Western United States, 1992–1993.” Morbidity and Mortality Weekly Report, vol. 42, no. 14, 16 Apr. 1993, pp. 258–63. Source record ↗

Government sourceGovernmentgovernment haccp
E09
1993The FDA revises the Food Code for restaurantsVERIFIED moderate

Evidence
In 1993 the FDA revised its Model Food Code for restaurants with new temperature guidelines for ground beef.

What it tells us
Restaurant cooking rules changed in the same year as the outbreak.

Why it matters
The Food Code is a model that states adopt, which is one way restaurant practice changes.

Claim it supports
Restaurant temperature guidance for ground beef changed in 1993.

Limitations
A later summary, not the Food Code itself. States adopt the code on their own schedules.

Full MLA source
Rangel, Josefa M., et al. “Epidemiology of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Outbreaks, United States, 1982–2002.” Emerging Infectious Diseases, vol. 11, no. 4, 2005, pp. 603–09. Source record ↗

Government sourceRestaurantsrestaurants regulation
E10
28 Mar. 1994Safe-handling labels become mandatoryVERIFIED moderateNeeds source verification

Evidence
FSIS made safe-handling instructions mandatory on all raw meat and poultry labels, covering storage, cross-contamination, cooking, and leftovers. Ground products had to comply by 27 May 1994.

What it tells us
Within about 14 months of the outbreak, a federal rule put cooking and handling warnings on raw meat packages.

Why it matters
It is a change ordinary shoppers could see. The timing is consistent with the outbreak as a trigger.

Claim it supports
A federal labeling rule followed the outbreak by about 14 months.

Limitations
That the outbreak caused this rule is inference. The rule's own stated reasons have not been read yet.

Full MLA source
United States, Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. “Mandatory Safe Handling Statements on Labeling of Raw Meat and Poultry Products.” Federal Register, vol. 59, no. 59, 28 Mar. 1994, p. 14528. Source record ↗

Government sourceRegulationregulation government
Needs source verification
E11
1994E. coli O157:H7 in ground beef becomes an “adulterant”VERIFIED strongNeeds source verification

Evidence
In 1994 FSIS began a sampling program that treated raw ground beef containing E. coli O157:H7 as adulterated, meaning illegal to sell. Supermarket and meat-industry groups sued, and on 13 December 1994 a federal court refused to block the program.

What it tells us
Before 1994, USDA had treated raw meat carrying pathogens as not adulterated. That changed for O157:H7.

Why it matters
A major legal shift, and the lawsuit shows that industry pushed back.

Claim it supports
In 1994 USDA began treating O157:H7 in raw ground beef as an adulterant, and a federal district court refused to block the program.

Limitations
The exact date of the announcement (reported as 28 Sept. 1994, by FSIS Administrator Michael Taylor) comes from secondary sources.

Full MLA source
Texas Food Industry Association v. Espy. 870 F. Supp. 143. United States District Court, Western District of Texas, 13 Dec. 1994. Source record ↗

Primary sourceRegulationregulation government industry
Needs source verification
E12
25 July 1996The 1996 Pathogen Reduction / HACCP ruleVERIFIED strong

Evidence
USDA's final rule required federally inspected meat and poultry plants to take preventive and corrective measures at each stage of production where food-safety hazards occur (HACCP), plus pathogen-reduction measures.

What it tells us
Responsibility for preventing contamination moved toward the companies, with USDA checking their systems.

Why it matters
This is the “1996 rules” at the end of the chain. It is a USDA regulation, not the “Pathogen Reduction Act.”

Claim it supports
In 1996 USDA required HACCP systems in federally inspected meat and poultry plants.

Limitations
Whether and how the rule's preamble cites the 1993 outbreak still needs to be read in the original.

Full MLA source
United States, Department of Agriculture, Food Safety and Inspection Service. “Pathogen Reduction; Hazard Analysis and Critical Control Point (HACCP) Systems; Final Rule.” Federal Register, vol. 61, 25 July 1996, p. 38806. Source record ↗

Government sourceRegulationregulation haccp industry
E13
2018Insiders: the outbreak accelerated work begun in 1992INTERPRETATION moderateNeeds source verification

Evidence
Murano, Cross and Riggs write that preparatory work on HACCP and risk-based inspection began in 1992, and that the outbreak accelerated mandatory HACCP. They also report that the outbreak was discussed at President Clinton's first cabinet meeting.

What it tells us
Officials who were there describe the outbreak as an accelerator, not the starting point.

Why it matters
This is the strongest single piece of evidence for “trigger, not sole cause.”

Claim it supports
The outbreak sped up a change that was already being prepared.

Limitations
Written 25 years later by people with a stake in how the reforms are remembered. The cabinet-meeting detail needs a primary source.

Full MLA source
Murano, Elsa A., et al. “The Outbreak That Changed Meat and Poultry Inspection Systems Worldwide.” Animal Frontiers, vol. 8, no. 4, 2018, pp. 4–8. Source record ↗

Secondary historical analysisGovernmentgovernment haccp historians
Needs source verification
E14
2000Four stages of meat-safety standardsINTERPRETATION moderate

Evidence
Juska et al. divide U.S. standards into stages: before 1982, after O157:H7 was identified in 1982, after the 1993 outbreak, and after the 1996 rules. They explain the money, politics and science behind each change.

What it tells us
Researchers treat 1993 as one turning point inside a longer process.

Why it matters
It gives the investigation its structure, and a way to test how much 1993 itself explains.

Claim it supports
Meat-safety standards changed in several stages driven by science, politics and economics.

Limitations
Sociologists writing for academics. Their framework is an argument, not a neutral timeline.

Full MLA source
Juska, Arunas, et al. “Negotiating Bacteriological Meat Contamination Standards in the US: The Case of E. coli O157:H7.” Sociologia Ruralis, vol. 40, no. 2, Apr. 2000, pp. 249–71. Source record ↗

Academic researchHistorianshistorians science government
E15
2003Concentration made the system vulnerableINTERPRETATION moderate

Evidence
Juska et al. argue that although beef is in some ways safer than in the past, the concentration of the meat industry since the 1980s made it more exposed to fast-spreading outbreaks. They question how well HACCP works.

What it tells us
Some researchers see the outbreak as a product of the system, not an accident.

Why it matters
If true, the outbreak was a symptom, and the deeper cause continued after 1996.

Claim it supports
Industrial concentration made outbreaks like 1993 more likely.

Limitations
Strongly critical of industry, national in scope, and ends in 2003.

Full MLA source
Juska, Arunas, et al. “Manufacturing Bacteriological Contamination Outbreaks in Industrialized Meat Production Systems: The Case of E. coli O157:H7.” Agriculture and Human Values, vol. 20, no. 1, Mar. 2003, pp. 3–19. Source record ↗

Academic researchMeat industryindustry historians continuity
E16
2007HACCP moved inspection onto the companiesINTERPRETATION moderate

Evidence
Dunn argues that under HACCP companies watch their own production instead of federal inspectors checking every carcass, and connects the start of this system to the Jack in the Box outbreak.

What it tells us
The change was not simply “more inspection.” It was a different kind of inspection.

Why it matters
It shows how a regulatory change can carry new risks of its own.

Claim it supports
HACCP shifted monitoring responsibility from federal inspectors to companies.

Limitations
A geographer's argument for academics, focused on USDA in the 2000s, not a plain timeline.

Full MLA source
Dunn, Elizabeth. “Escherichia coli, Corporate Discipline and the Failure of the Sewer State.” Space and Polity, vol. 11, no. 1, Apr. 2007, pp. 35–53. Source record ↗

Academic researchHistorianshaccp historians continuity
E17
1982–2002Outbreaks continued, but not from fast-food burgersVERIFIED strong

Evidence
CDC researchers counted 350 O157:H7 outbreaks in the U.S. from 1982 to 2002: 8,598 cases and 40 deaths. 183 outbreaks were foodborne, and 75 of those (41%) were linked to ground beef. They report no fast-food hamburger outbreaks since 1995.

What it tells us
One kind of outbreak became rare after the reforms, while O157:H7 outbreaks overall did not disappear.

Why it matters
This is the core evidence for both change and continuity.

Claim it supports
After 1995, fast-food hamburger outbreaks stopped being reported, but O157:H7 outbreaks continued from other sources.

Limitations
Outbreak reports depend on detection and reporting, which also improved. Fewer reports does not prove fewer illnesses on its own.

Full MLA source
Rangel, Josefa M., et al. “Epidemiology of Escherichia coli O157:H7 Outbreaks, United States, 1982–2002.” Emerging Infectious Diseases, vol. 11, no. 4, 2005, pp. 603–09. Source record ↗

Government sourceContinuitycontinuity restaurants industry
E18
2018A reported 46% drop in infections by 2004INTERPRETATION limitedNeeds source verification

Evidence
Murano et al. report that rates of E. coli O157:H7 infection fell 46% by 2004.

What it tells us
Officials connected to the reforms point to a large decline in infections.

Why it matters
If the figure holds, it is strong evidence that the post-1993 changes reduced risk.

Claim it supports
Infection rates fell substantially after the reforms.

Limitations
The original data (likely CDC surveillance) has not been checked. The baseline year and the cause of the drop are not established here.

Full MLA source
Murano, Elsa A., et al. “The Outbreak That Changed Meat and Poultry Inspection Systems Worldwide.” Animal Frontiers, vol. 8, no. 4, 2018, pp. 4–8. Source record ↗

Secondary historical analysisContinuitycontinuity historians
Needs source verification
E19
1993Washington's cooking rule and the chain's practiceUNRESOLVED uncertainNeeds source verification

Evidence
What temperature did Washington State require for hamburgers before the outbreak, and did chain A meet it? The sources gathered so far do not say.

What it tells us
Nothing yet. This is a gap in the evidence.

Why it matters
It decides whether the outbreak was a failure to follow existing rules, or a failure of the rules themselves.

Claim it supports
Unknown: whether the chain was meeting the state's cooking requirement.

Limitations
Needs Washington State Department of Health records or Bell et al. (1994).

Full MLA source
No source found yet. This is a gap in the research.

FOLLOW THE CHAIN

How much evidence connects one moment to the next?

Each arrow opens the reading, the linked exhibits, the causal-strength stamp and the question the record cannot settle.

1982–83E. coli O157:H7 recognized as a foodborne threat
1992–93The Jack in the Box outbreak
1993Public attention and political pressure
1993–94Government response
1996Changes in meat-safety regulation
1996 →Changes in industry practices
1995 → todayLong-term consequences

LINK 01 · 1982–83 → 1992–93

E. coli O157:H7 recognized as a foodborne threat → The Jack in the Box outbreak

What evidence connects these moments? Recognition did not cause the outbreak. It made the outbreak detectable.

moderate Causal strength

Linked exhibits E01 E02 E03

What we still cannot prove
Whether the outbreak would have been identified so fast without the 1982 discovery, or whether earlier action on that knowledge could have prevented it.

LINK 02 · 1992–93 → 1993

The Jack in the Box outbreak → Public attention and political pressure

What evidence connects these moments? Children's deaths and a multistate recall made the outbreak national news inside government.

moderate Causal strength

Linked exhibits E06 E04 E13

What we still cannot prove
How strong public pressure really was. No newspaper coverage, polling, or advocacy-group records have been gathered yet.

LINK 03 · 1993 → 1993–94

Public attention and political pressure → Government response

What evidence connects these moments? Federal actions followed quickly, but some were already in motion.

moderate Causal strength

Linked exhibits E07 E08 E09 E10 E13

What we still cannot prove
Whether these actions would have happened anyway, only later. The critical-control-point work predates the outbreak.

LINK 04 · 1993–94 → 1996

Government response → Changes in meat-safety regulation

What evidence connects these moments? The 1994 adulterant policy and the 1996 HACCP rule are the clearest regulatory changes.

moderate Causal strength

Linked exhibits E11 E12 E13 E16

What we still cannot prove
What the 1996 rule's own preamble says about the outbreak. It has not been read yet.

LINK 05 · 1996 → 1996 →

Changes in meat-safety regulation → Changes in industry practices

What evidence connects these moments? Plants had a legal duty to adopt HACCP, so the regulation directly required new practice.

strong Causal strength

Linked exhibits E12 E16 E09

What we still cannot prove
How individual restaurant chains changed their kitchens. No company source has been gathered.

LINK 06 · 1996 → → 1995 → today

Changes in industry practices → Long-term consequences

What evidence connects these moments? Fast-food burger outbreaks stopped being reported, but outbreaks from other sources continued.

limited Causal strength

Linked exhibits E17 E18 E15

What we still cannot prove
That the reforms, rather than better cooking, testing or reporting, caused the decline.
